articles.title: Fed Chair Warsh warns inflation progress has stalled in first Jackson Hole address
articles.excerpt: In his highest-profile speech since taking over the central bank, Warsh declined to signal the Fed's next move, and traders raised their bets on a September rate hike.
articles.author: fiveboroughbulletin-staff
content: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh used his first Jackson Hole address as chair to warn that recent progress on inflation may be less durable than it appears, in a speech that offered investors little of the forward guidance many had been hoping for.

Speaking at the Kansas City Fed's annual symposium in Wyoming, roughly a hundred days into his tenure, Warsh acknowledged that summer inflation readings had come in somewhat better than expected but argued the underlying trend has not clearly improved enough to declare victory. He suggested the central bank could still need to raise rates further if price pressures fail to ease in the months ahead.

Warsh was notably light on specifics about the Fed's next steps, telling the audience they could describe his approach as a general outline or a rough map of his thinking, but stopped short of calling it formal forward guidance, a term that carries specific weight in how markets interpret central bank communication.

That ambiguity had an immediate effect on trading floors. Futures markets tracked by the CME Group's FedWatch tool showed the probability of a quarter-point rate increase at the Fed's mid-September meeting roughly double from about a third to near a coin flip in the hours after the speech, as traders repriced the odds of a more hawkish path.

The tone marked a contrast with the Jackson Hole speech delivered by Warsh's predecessor a year earlier, which had leaned dovish and helped fuel a stock market rally. Warsh's more cautious framing instead left investors parsing his remarks for clues rather than taking comfort from a clear signal in either direction.

Economists said the speech reflected the difficult position facing the Fed as it weighs still-elevated inflation against signs of a cooling labor market, a balancing act that has left policymakers publicly divided over whether the next move should be a cut, a hike, or no change at all when the committee meets next month.

articles.title: S&P 500 tops 7,800 for the first time as August rally extends
articles.excerpt: Cooling inflation data and strong corporate earnings pushed all three major U.S. indexes to fresh records within the same trading week.
articles.author: fiveboroughbulletin-staff
content: The S&P 500 closed above 7,800 for the first time this week, extending an August rally that has carried all three major U.S. stock indexes to fresh record territory within the span of a few trading sessions.

The milestone followed the Dow Jones Industrial Average's own first close above 54,000 earlier in the month, while the Nasdaq Composite has repeatedly set new highs of its own as technology shares continued to lead the broader market higher.

Investors pointed to a combination of factors behind the run, chief among them a string of inflation readings that came in cooler than economists had expected, easing some of the pressure that had weighed on markets earlier in the year. Corporate earnings for the second quarter also came in broadly stronger than forecast, particularly among large technology companies whose results carry outsized weight in the major indexes.

Falling oil prices and a partial easing of tensions in the Middle East also helped support risk appetite, traders said, reducing some of the geopolitical premium that had been built into energy and defense-adjacent stocks earlier in the summer.

Even so, strategists cautioned that markets remain sensitive to any signs of a policy shift from the Federal Reserve, noting that a large share of the year's gains have been concentrated in a small number of dominant technology companies. Any disappointment in upcoming earnings from that group, they said, could quickly test the resilience of the broader rally.

Trading volumes were described as moderate for the milestone, consistent with a summer market that has drifted steadily higher rather than surging on any single catalyst, a pattern several analysts said reflects broad but cautious optimism rather than outright exuberance.

articles.title: Treasury doubles bond buybacks as national debt tops $40 trillion for the first time
articles.excerpt: The surprise move came days after the 30-year yield hit its highest level since 2007, and briefly sent longer-term borrowing costs lower.
articles.author: fiveboroughbulletin-staff
content: The U.S. Treasury Department said this week it will at least double the size of its bond buyback operations, a surprise intervention aimed at easing pressure on longer-term borrowing costs after the 30-year yield touched its highest level since 2007.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's department said it would raise the size of each buyback operation to at least $4 billion from $2 billion, targeting securities in the 10-to-30-year range starting in September and running into early November. The announcement came the same week official figures showed the national debt had climbed above $40 trillion for the first time.

The initial market reaction was sharp: the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield fell from around 4.68 percent to as low as 4.63 percent, while the 30-year yield dropped from roughly 5.26 percent to about 5.18 percent, as the prospect of the government stepping in as a larger buyer of its own long-dated debt eased some of the recent selling pressure.

That relief proved only partial. Yields on both securities drifted back up the following day as traders weighed the buyback plan against the broader forces that had pushed borrowing costs higher in the first place, including concerns about a widening budget deficit, inflation that has stayed above the Fed's target, and a wave of corporate bond issuance competing with Treasuries for investor demand.

Analysts described the buyback increase as a targeted, short-term tool rather than a structural fix for the pressures facing the bond market, noting that the government still needs to finance the same underlying deficit regardless of how it manages the mix of debt maturities it issues.

The episode added to a summer of unusually active involvement by the Treasury in the mechanics of the bond market, with officials signaling they are prepared to use further buybacks or other tools if long-term yields continue climbing toward levels that could ripple into mortgage rates and other consumer borrowing costs.

articles.title: Gold climbs to a three-month high as investors brace for Jackson Hole
articles.excerpt: Bullion's steady August climb reflects a mix of central bank buying, bond market jitters and anticipation of the Fed chair's speech.
articles.author: fiveboroughbulletin-staff
articles.imageCaption: Gold bars at a bullion dealer
content: Gold prices climbed to their highest level in more than three months this week, extending a steady run higher through August as investors positioned themselves ahead of the Federal Reserve's Jackson Hole symposium and a fresh round of inflation data.

December gold futures opened Tuesday just above $4,710 an ounce, building on a rally that has taken the metal from around $4,000 at the start of the month to its strongest levels since the spring. The advance has come in fits and starts, with notable jumps following the Treasury's decision to expand its bond buyback program and after minutes from the Fed's most recent policy meeting were released.

Traders pointed to several forces reinforcing the move. Persistent geopolitical tension in the Middle East has kept a steady bid under gold as a traditional haven asset, while uncertainty over the path of interest rates has made the non-yielding metal relatively more attractive compared with bonds whose returns have been swinging along with Treasury market volatility.

Central bank buying has also provided a structural tailwind. Data from the World Gold Council showed official-sector purchases in the second quarter running well above year-earlier levels, as a number of central banks continued to diversify reserves away from a heavy concentration in the U.S. dollar.

Analysts said the timing of the latest high was no coincidence, coming just days before the Fed chair's highly anticipated Jackson Hole remarks and the release of the central bank's preferred inflation gauge. Any signal that the Fed is prepared to hold rates higher for longer, they said, could either dent gold's momentum by lifting the dollar or extend the rally further if it stokes broader market uncertainty.

Precious metals traders cautioned that gold's gains this year have already outpaced expectations set at the start of 2026, and some warned that a sharp reversal is possible if incoming data reduces the current level of economic uncertainty.
